claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 3D-E.

claims.claim: The ratios of the YFP-marked luminal to basal subsets were significantly reduced in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
claims.source: Furthermore, the ratios of the YFP-marked luminal to basal subsets were also significantly reduced in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females (Figure 3D,F)
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 3D and 3F.

claims.claim: The reduction in the YFP+ luminal/basal ratio was most likely due to a reduction in the YFP-marked Runx1-null luminal population.
claims.source: However, since the overall population of YFP+ MECs in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was reduced (Figure 3D–E), the reduction in the YFP+ luminal/basal ratio was most likely due to a reduction in the YFP-marked Runx1-null luminal population.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the overall reduction in YFP+ MECs.

claims.claim: Most breast cancers, including both basal-like and luminal subtypes, may originate from luminal cells, rather than from basal MaSCs.
claims.source: Recent studies suggest that most breast cancers, including both basal-like and luminal subtypes, may originate from luminal cells, rather than from basal MaSCs (Lim et al., 2009; Molyneux et al., 2010; Proia et al., 2011; Keller et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to four studies.

claims.claim: RUNX1 and CBFB mutations have only been found in the luminal subtype of human breast cancers.
claims.source: Furthermore, RUNX1 and CBFB mutations have only been found in the luminal subtype of human breast cancers (Banerji et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Ellis et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to three sequencing studies.

claims.claim: GSEA showed significant enrichment of a previously generated LP signature and downregulation of a ML signature in Runx1-null luminal cells.
claims.source: By gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA [Subramanian et al., 2005]), we observed significant enrichment of a previously generated LP signature and downregulation of a ML signature in Runx1-null luminal cells (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Significant enrichment of multiple gene sets related to p53 signaling was observed in Runx1-null luminal cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, we also observed significant enrichment of multiple gene sets related to p53 signaling in Runx1-null luminal cells in relation to Runx1-WT luminal cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), possibly indicating a stress response in these mutant luminal cells in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Elf5 was upregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells.
claims.source: In our microarray data, we found that Elf5, a TF gene critically required in the alveolar cell lineage and a LP marker (Oakes et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2009; Lim et al., 2010), was upregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Several ductal luminal TF/co-factor genes (e.g., Gata3, Foxa1, Esr1, Cited1) were downregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells.
claims.source: whereas several ductal luminal TF/co-factor genes (e.g., Gata3, Foxa1, Esr1, Cited1) were downregulated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Expression levels of Foxa1, Esr1, and Cited1 were downregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells by qRT-PCR validation.
claims.source: When validated by qRT-PCR, we found that although the expression of Gata3 did not seem to be significantly affected in luminal cells upon Runx1-loss, expression levels of Foxa1, Esr1, and Cited1 were downregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells, whereas Elf5 expression was upregulated (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Elf5 expression was upregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells by qRT-PCR validation.
claims.source: When validated by qRT-PCR, we found that although the expression of Gata3 did not seem to be significantly affected in luminal cells upon Runx1-loss, expression levels of Foxa1, Esr1, and Cited1 were downregulated in Runx1-null luminal cells, whereas Elf5 expression was upregulated (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The YFP+ Runx1-null CD14−c-Kit− ML subpopulation was significantly reduced in both pubertal and adult virgin MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
claims.source: Intriguingly, we found that in both pubertal and adult virgin MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females, the YFP+ Runx1-null ML subpopulation defined based on CD14 and c-Kit staining (Lin−CD24+CD29loCD14−c-Kit−, referred to as CD14−c-Kit− MLs hereafter) (Asselin-Labat et al., 2011) was significantly reduced, whereas the YFP+ Runx1-null LP subpopulation (Lin−CD24+CD29loCD14+c-Kit+, referred to as CD14+c-Kit+ LPs hereafter) was increased (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 4C-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claims.claim: The YFP+ Runx1-null LP subpopulation was increased in both pubertal and adult virgin MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
claims.source: Intriguingly, we found that in both pubertal and adult virgin MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females, the YFP+ Runx1-null ML subpopulation defined based on CD14 and c-Kit staining (Lin−CD24+CD29loCD14−c-Kit−, referred to as CD14−c-Kit− MLs hereafter) (Asselin-Labat et al., 2011) was significantly reduced, whereas the YFP+ Runx1-null LP subpopulation (Lin−CD24+CD29loCD14+c-Kit+, referred to as CD14+c-Kit+ LPs hereafter) was increased (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 4C-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claims.claim: Runx1 expression in YFP+ LPs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was significantly reduced.
claims.source: By qRT-PCR, we found that while Runx1 expression in YFP+ LPs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was significantly reduced, its expression in YFP-marked MLs was only slightly reduced (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Runx1 expression in YFP-marked MLs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was only slightly reduced.
claims.source: By qRT-PCR, we found that while Runx1 expression in YFP+ LPs from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females was significantly reduced, its expression in YFP-marked MLs was only slightly reduced (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Many YFP+ MLs in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females might have escaped Cre-mediated excision in at least one copy of their Runx1L alleles.
claims.source: This data suggested that many YFP+ MLs in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females might have escaped Cre-mediated excision in at least one copy of their Runx1L alleles (thus they were either Runx1+/+ or Runx1+/−).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the qRT-PCR data showing only slight reduction in Runx1 expression in YFP+ MLs.

claims.claim: RUNX1 is essential for the emergence or maintenance of the ML lineage.
claims.source: The data thus also suggests that RUNX1 is essential for the emergence or maintenance of the ML lineage.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that YFP+ MLs appear to have escaped Runx1 deletion.

claims.claim: The luminal cell compartment of the mouse MG can be resolved into non-clonogenic ER+ MLs, as well as clonogenic ER+ LPs and ER− LPs based on CD49b and Sca1 staining.
claims.source: A recent study demonstrated that the luminal cell compartment of the mouse MG could be further resolved into non-clonogenic ER+ MLs, as well as clonogenic ER+ LPs and ER− LPs based on CD49b and Sca1 staining; the ER+ LPs may represent progenitors for ER+ MLs whereas the ER− LPs probably represent alveolar progenitors (Shehata et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Shehata et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The CD49b−Sca1+ ER+ ML subpopulation was significantly reduced in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
claims.source: We found that compared to their corresponding subpopulations in MMTV-Cre;Runx1+/+;R26Y control females, the CD49b−Sca1+ ER+ ML subpopulation was significantly reduced in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 4F-G.

claims.claim: The CD49b+Sca1− ER− LP subpopulation was significantly increased in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
claims.source: whereas the CD49b+Sca1− ER− LP subpopulation was significantly increased
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 4F-G.

claims.claim: The CD49b+Sca1+ ER+ LP subpopulation was not significantly altered in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y females.
claims.source: the CD49b+Sca1+ ER+ LP subpopulation was not significantly altered (Figure 4F–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 4F-G.

claims.claim: The YFP-marked ER− LP subset had a profound reduction in Runx1 expression.
claims.source: We found that whereas the YFP-marked ER− LP subset had a profound reduction in Runx1 expression, the YFP+ ER+ LP subset exhibited a partial reduction in Runx1 transcripts, and the YFP+ ER+ ML subpopulation had almost no loss of Runx1 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: The YFP+ ER+ LP subset exhibited a partial reduction in Runx1 transcripts.
claims.source: We found that whereas the YFP-marked ER− LP subset had a profound reduction in Runx1 expression, the YFP+ ER+ LP subset exhibited a partial reduction in Runx1 transcripts, and the YFP+ ER+ ML subpopulation had almost no loss of Runx1 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: The YFP+ ER+ ML subpopulation had almost no loss of Runx1 expression.
claims.source: We found that whereas the YFP-marked ER− LP subset had a profound reduction in Runx1 expression, the YFP+ ER+ LP subset exhibited a partial reduction in Runx1 transcripts, and the YFP+ ER+ ML subpopulation had almost no loss of Runx1 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: RUNX1 is required for the development or maintenance of the ER+ luminal lineage.
claims.source: Collectively, our data suggest that RUNX1 is required for the development or maintenance of the ER+ luminal lineage, and it is particularly essential for the ER+ MLs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined FACS and expression data.

claims.claim: RUNX1 is particularly essential for the ER+ MLs.
claims.source: Collectively, our data suggest that RUNX1 is required for the development or maintenance of the ER+ luminal lineage, and it is particularly essential for the ER+ MLs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined FACS and expression data.

claims.claim: Pathway signatures of RB1 mutation, TP53 mutation, and RUNX1 mutation are co-associated with human luminal B breast tumors.
claims.source: Interestingly, one recent sequencing study unveiled that pathway signatures of RB1 mutation, TP53 mutation, and RUNX1 mutation are co-associated with human luminal B breast tumors (Ellis et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ellis et al., 2012.

claims.claim: >50% of luminal breast cancer cases with RUNX1 mutations are accompanied by mutations or deletions in either TP53 or RB1 genes.
claims.source: Furthermore, by carefully examining luminal breast cancer cases with RUNX1 mutations, we noticed that >50% of them are accompanied by mutations or deletions in either TP53 or RB1 genes (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of data from Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012.

claims.claim: Upon MMTV-Cre-induced Trp53 or Rb1 loss alone, the percentages of YFP-marked MECs increased dramatically.
claims.source: Upon MMTV-Cre-induced Trp53 or Rb1 loss alone, the percentages of YFP-marked MECs increased dramatically so that the majority of MECs in their MGs became YFP+ (Figure 5A, increased from ∼20–30% to ∼70–90%), suggesting a growth advantage for Trp53-null or Rb1-null MECs (in relation to their Trp53-WT or Rb1-WT YFP− neighbors).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Trp53-null or Rb1-null MECs have a growth advantage in relation to their WT neighbors.
claims.source: Upon MMTV-Cre-induced Trp53 or Rb1 loss alone, the percentages of YFP-marked MECs increased dramatically so that the majority of MECs in their MGs became YFP+ (Figure 5A, increased from ∼20–30% to ∼70–90%), suggesting a growth advantage for Trp53-null or Rb1-null MECs (in relation to their Trp53-WT or Rb1-WT YFP− neighbors).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the dramatic increase in YFP+ MECs upon Trp53 or Rb1 loss.

claims.claim: The percentages of the YFP-marked luminal population were reduced upon MMTV-Cre-induced Trp53 or Rb1 loss alone.
claims.source: However, the percentages of the YFP-marked luminal population were both reduced (Figure 5A, middle and bottom left plots compared to upper left plot, green circles).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Disruption of Runx1 together with Trp53 significantly increased the percentages of the YFP+ luminal population.
claims.source: Interestingly, disruption of Runx1 either together with Trp53 or with Rb1 significantly increased the percentages of the YFP+ luminal population (Figure 5A–C, increased from ∼4% [Trp53-loss alone] to ∼11% [Runx1/Trp53-loss] [Figure 5B]
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 5A-C.

claims.claim: Disruption of Runx1 together with Rb1 significantly increased the percentages of the YFP+ luminal population.
claims.source: Interestingly, disruption of Runx1 either together with Trp53 or with Rb1 significantly increased the percentages of the YFP+ luminal population (Figure 5A–C, increased from ∼4% [Trp53-loss alone] to ∼11% [Runx1/Trp53-loss] [Figure 5B] and from ∼12% [Rb1-loss alone] to ∼23% [Runx1/Rb1-loss] [Figure 5C], respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 5A-C.

claims.claim: The percentage of the YFP-marked ML subpopulation was reverted back to almost the normal level upon simultaneous loss of Runx1 together with either Trp53 or Rb1.
claims.source: Of particular note, the percentage of the YFP-marked ML subpopulation, which was dramatically reduced upon Runx1-loss alone (Figure 5A, upper right plot, red circle), was reverted back to almost the normal level upon simultaneous loss of Runx1 together with either Trp53 or Rb1 (Figure 5A, middle right plot for Trp53 [5B for quantification], bottom right plot for Rb1 [5C for quantification], red circles).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figures 5A-C.

claims.claim: Abundant ERα+ luminal MECs were detected in both MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Trp53L/L;R26Y and MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y compound females.
claims.source: To verify the presence of ER+ MECs in the MGs of these compound female mice, we performed IHC staining for ERα and could indeed detect abundant ERα+ luminal MECs in both MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Trp53L/L;R26Y and MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y compound females (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B
claims.evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: More than 50% reduction in Runx1 expression level was observed in the YFP-marked ML subpopulation sorted from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y females.
claims.source: By qRT-PCR analysis, we observed more than 50% reduction in the Runx1 expression level in the YFP-marked ML subpopulation sorted from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y females (Figure 5D), suggesting a significant portion of these YFP+ MLs should have undergone biallelic excision of their Runx1L alleles.
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: A significant portion of YFP+ MLs in MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y females should have undergone biallelic excision of their Runx1L alleles.
claims.source: By qRT-PCR analysis, we observed more than 50% reduction in the Runx1 expression level in the YFP-marked ML subpopulation sorted from MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;Rb1L/L;R26Y females (Figure 5D), suggesting a significant portion of these YFP+ MLs should have undergone biallelic excision of their Runx1L alleles.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the >50% reduction in Runx1 expression.

claims.claim: RUNX1 knockdown stable lines could only be obtained from TP53-mutant T47D cells but not from TP53-WT MCF7 cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, despite multiple attempts, we were only able to obtain RUNX1 knockdown (kd) stable lines from TP53-mutant T47D cells but not from TP53-WT MCF7 cells.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from cell culture experiments.

claims.claim: A similar genetic interaction between RUNX1-loss and TP53-loss may also operate in human ER+ luminal breast cells.
claims.source: This observation suggests that a similar genetic interaction between RUNX1-loss and TP53-loss may also operate in human ER+ luminal breast cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the inability to obtain RUNX1 knockdown in TP53-WT cells.

claims.claim: Upon RUNX1 knockdown in T47D cells, the protein level of ELF5 was increased.
claims.source: By Western blot, we found that upon RUNX1 kd, the protein level of ELF5 was increased, whereas the protein levels of both ERα and FOXA1 were reduced, and CITED1 protein level appeared unchanged (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Upon RUNX1 knockdown in T47D cells, the protein levels of both ERα and FOXA1 were reduced.
claims.source: By Western blot, we found that upon RUNX1 kd, the protein level of ELF5 was increased, whereas the protein levels of both ERα and FOXA1 were reduced, and CITED1 protein level appeared unchanged (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Upon RUNX1 knockdown in T47D cells, CITED1 protein level appeared unchanged.
claims.source: By Western blot, we found that upon RUNX1 kd, the protein level of ELF5 was increased, whereas the protein levels of both ERα and FOXA1 were reduced, and CITED1 protein level appeared unchanged (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: RUNX1 was shown as a direct target of ELF5 and is repressed by it, based on chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis.
claims.source: Interestingly, it was shown previously that RUNX1 is a direct target of ELF5 and is repressed by it, based on chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis (Kalyuga et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalyuga et al., 2012.

claims.claim: A largely opposite expression pattern of Elf5 and Runx1 was observed in microarray data for sorted MEC subsets.
claims.source: In our microarray data for sorted MEC subsets, as well as those publicly available microarray datasets we analyzed, we could always observe a largely opposite expression pattern of Elf5 and Runx1 (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In basal cells and MLs in which Runx1 is highly expressed, Elf5 is not expressed.
claims.source: In both basal cells and MLs in which Runx1 is highly expressed, Elf5 is not; Elf5 expression is greatly elevated in ALs whereas Runx1 expression is repressed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Elf5 expression is greatly elevated in ALs whereas Runx1 expression is repressed.
claims.source: In both basal cells and MLs in which Runx1 is highly expressed, Elf5 is not; Elf5 expression is greatly elevated in ALs whereas Runx1 expression is repressed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Upon induction of alveolar differentiation in HC11 cells, the ELF5 protein level was increased, whereas the RUNX1 protein level was reduced.
claims.source: This negative correlation in their expression levels could be further confirmed in the HC11 cell line model. While both Runx1 and Elf5 were expressed in uninduced HC11 cells, upon induction of alveolar differentiation, the ELF5 protein level was increased, whereas the RUNX1 protein level was reduced (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Significant binding of RUNX1 to multiple evolutionary conserved RUNX-binding sites in the ELF5 locus was identified by ChIP analysis.
claims.source: To determine whether ELF5 is also a direct target of RUNX1, we performed ChIP analysis on T47D cells and identified significant binding of RUNX1 to multiple evolutionary conserved RUNX-binding sites in the ELF5 locus (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: RUNX1-binding was particularly profound in an enhancer region ∼17 kb upstream of the ELF5 transcription start site (ECR-1).
claims.source: The RUNX1-binding was particularly profound in an enhancer region ∼17 kb upstream of the ELF5 transcription start site (ECR-1, Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Significant binding of RUNX1 to the −1.6 kb and −1.9 kb motifs in the FOXA1 locus was confirmed by ChIP assay.
claims.source: By ChIP assay, we confirmed significant binding of RUNX1 to the −1.6 kb and −1.9 kb motifs in the FOXA1 locus (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: FOXA1 and ELF5 genes may be direct targets of RUNX1 positively and negatively regulated by it, respectively.
claims.source: Collectively, these data suggest that FOXA1 and ELF5 genes may be direct targets of RUNX1 positively and negatively regulated by it, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP and expression data.

claims.claim: Both Elf5 and Esr1 appeared upregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs from Rb1/Runx1 double mutants compared to Rb1 single mutants.
claims.source: When comparing double mutants (with Rb1/Runx1-loss) to single mutants (with Rb1-loss alone), we found that both Elf5 and Esr1 appeared upregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs (based on CD49 and Sca1 staining) from double mutants (Figure 7A–B, left plots)
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 7A-B.

claims.claim: Foxa1 and Cited1 were downregulated in the rescued double mutant ER+ MLs compared to Rb1 single mutants.
claims.source: and Foxa1 and Cited1 were downregulated in the rescued double mutant ER+ MLs (Figure 7B, left plot).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Both Elf5 and Esr1 were upregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs from double mutants compared to WT females.
claims.source: From this comparison, we found that both Elf5 and Esr1 were also upregulated and Foxa1 and Cited1 were slightly downregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs from double mutants (Figure 7A–B, right plots).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 7A-B.

claims.claim: Foxa1 and Cited1 were slightly downregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs from double mutants compared to WT females.
claims.source: From this comparison, we found that both Elf5 and Esr1 were also upregulated and Foxa1 and Cited1 were slightly downregulated in ER+ LPs and ER+ MLs from double mutants (Figure 7A–B, right plots).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figures 7A-B.

claims.claim: In Runx1-mutant ER+ LPs, both Elf5 and Esr1 were upregulated and Foxa1 and Cited1 also appeared slightly upregulated.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that in Runx1-mutant ER+ LPs both Elf5 and Esr1 were upregulated and Foxa1 and Cited1 also appeared slightly upregulated (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: In older Rb1-null single mutants, Esr1, Foxa1, and Cited1 were upregulated and Elf5 was downregulated in their YFP+ CD14−c-Kit− MLs.
claims.source: By using this strategy, we found that in Rb1-null single mutants (controls), Esr1, Foxa1, and Cited1 were upregulated and Elf5 was downregulated in their YFP+ CD14−c-Kit− MLs when they aged

claims.claim: In YFP+ MLs from double mutants, following Runx1 reduction, although Esr1 was upregulated to a similar level, Foxa1 and Cited1 were not, and Elf5 was even further upregulated.
claims.source: however, in YFP+ MLs from double mutants, following Runx1 reduction, although Esr1 was upregulated to a similar level (to that of single mutants), Foxa1 and Cited1 were not, and Elf5 was even further upregulated (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time course qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: A similar trend of changes for Foxa1, Cited1, and Elf5 was observed in YFP+ CD14+c-Kit+ LPs from the same animals.
claims.source: We also observed a similar trend of changes for Foxa1, Cited1, and Elf5 in YFP+ CD14+c-Kit+ LPs from the same animals (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time course qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: In ER+ luminal cells, RUNX1 negatively and positively regulates the expression of Elf5 and mature luminal TF/co-factor genes (e.g., Foxa1 and Cited1), respectively.
claims.source: Overall, the data from this time course study further supports that in ER+ luminal cells, RUNX1 negatively and positively regulates the expression of Elf5 and mature luminal TF/co-factor genes (e.g., Foxa1 and Cited1), respectively.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the time course expression data.

claims.claim: Differentiation of ER+ luminal MECs requires coordinated expression of these factors and Runx1-loss may disrupt their coordinated expression.

claims.evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern data.

claims.claim: Elf5 is a key target gene of RUNX1 repressed by it in MECs.
claims.source: Collectively, our in vitro and in vivo expression analyses coupled with ChIP analysis suggest that Elf5 is a key target gene of RUNX1 repressed by it in MECs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP and expression data.

claims.claim: Foxa1 is a direct target of RUNX1.
claims.source: RUNX1 also positively regulates the expression of mature luminal TF/co-factor genes involved in the ER program and among them, Foxa1 is a direct target of RUNX1
claims.evidence: This is inferred from ChIP data showing RUNX1 binding to FOXA1 regulatory regions.

claims.claim: RUNX1 does not appear to regulate transcription of Esr1 directly.
claims.source: and RUNX1 does not appear to regulate transcription of Esr1 directly.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of consistent downregulation of Esr1 in vivo and the pattern of Esr1 upregulation.

claims.claim: GATA3 has been shown as a common master regulator for both ER+ ductal luminal cells and ER− alveolar luminal cells.
claims.source: Among TFs that control cell fates of the two subpopulations of luminal MECs, GATA3 has been shown as a common master regulator for both ER+ ductal luminal cells and ER− alveolar luminal cells (Kouros-Mehr et al., 2006; Asselin-Labat et al., 2007)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to two studies.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to two studies.

claims.claim: RUNX1 is a key regulator of ER+ luminal MECs.
claims.source: In this study, we identified RUNX1 as a key regulator of ER+ luminal MECs.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: RUNX1 controls the in vivo fate of ER+ luminal cells by repressing the program for an alternative cell fate choice (i.e., repressing the key TF gene for alveolar cells, Elf5).

results.result: Runx1 is expressed in all mammary epithelial cell (MEC) subpopulations except secretory alveolar luminal cells. This expression pattern was confirmed through multiple methods including qRT-PCR, immunohistochemistry, and microarray analysis across different developmental stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C21-C28 collectively demonstrate Runx1 expression patterns through convergent evidence from qRT-PCR (C21, C28), IHC staining (C22-C25), and microarray profiling (C26-C27). The data consistently show expression in luminal and basal cells but absence in alveolar luminal cells, with appropriate controls and multiple independent validation methods.

results.result: Conditional knockout of Runx1 in MECs using MMTV-Cre leads to a profound reduction in ER+ mature luminal cells. FACS analysis revealed significant decreases in the YFP+ luminal population, particularly the CD14−c-Kit− mature luminal and CD49b−Sca1+ ER+ ML subpopulations. qRT-PCR analysis of residual YFP+ MLs showed only slight Runx1 reduction, suggesting these cells escaped Cre-mediated excision, indicating RUNX1 is essential for ER+ luminal cell maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C32-C64 provide comprehensive FACS and qRT-PCR evidence demonstrating reduction in ER+ luminal cells upon Runx1 knockout. The observation that residual YFP+ MLs retain Runx1 expression (C53, C62) strongly supports essentiality. Multiple independent sorting strategies (CD14/c-Kit and CD49b/Sca1) converge on the same conclusion with appropriate statistical analysis.

results.result: Loss of either Trp53 or Rb1 rescues the ER+ luminal cell reduction phenotype caused by Runx1 knockout. In double mutant mice (Runx1/Trp53 or Runx1/Rb1 loss), the percentage of YFP+ mature luminal cells was restored to near-normal levels, with >50% reduction in Runx1 expression confirmed by qRT-PCR, indicating genuine biallelic excision in rescued cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C67-C75 demonstrate genetic rescue through FACS analysis showing restoration of ML populations in double mutants (C70-C72) and qRT-PCR confirmation of Runx1 loss in rescued cells (C74-C75). IHC validation confirms presence of ERα+ cells (C73). The dramatic increase in YFP+ luminal cells from ~4% to ~11% (Trp53) and ~12% to ~23% (Rb1) provides strong quantitative support.

results.result: RUNX1 directly represses Elf5, a master regulator of alveolar cells. ChIP analysis identified significant RUNX1 binding to multiple conserved sites in the ELF5 locus, particularly a region ~17 kb upstream. Upon Runx1 loss, Elf5 expression was upregulated in luminal cells and dramatically de-repressed in basal cells where it is normally not expressed, demonstrating RUNX1 represses Elf5 across multiple MEC subsets.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C46, C48-C49, C78, C82-C87, C102, C108, C114-C116 provide convergent evidence from ChIP-qPCR (C86-C87), Western blot (C78), qRT-PCR in vivo (C46, C48-C49, C115), and microarray data (C82-C84) demonstrating direct repression. The profound upregulation of Elf5 in basal cells upon Runx1 loss (C115) where it is normally absent provides particularly strong evidence for direct repression.

results.result: RUNX1 positively regulates mature luminal transcription factor/co-factor genes involved in the ER program, including Foxa1 and Cited1. ChIP analysis confirmed direct RUNX1 binding to FOXA1 regulatory regions. Time-course analysis in rescued double mutants showed that while Esr1 was upregulated, Foxa1 and Cited1 failed to upregulate properly upon Runx1 reduction, supporting positive regulation by RUNX1.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C47-C48, C88-C98, C103, C109 demonstrate positive regulation through ChIP evidence for direct binding to FOXA1 (C88), expression analysis showing downregulation upon Runx1 loss (C47-C48, C91), and time-course studies in double mutants (C95-C97) that control for genetic background effects. The convergence of in vitro (C79) and in vivo (C91, C96) data strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Gene set enrichment analysis of Runx1-null luminal cells showed significant enrichment of luminal progenitor signatures, downregulation of mature luminal signatures, and enrichment of p53 signaling pathway gene sets, suggesting a stress response in mutant luminal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 present GSEA results with appropriate statistical significance (p<0.001, FDR q-values reported). The enrichment of p53 pathway genes is consistent with the genetic rescue experiments and provides mechanistic insight. However, C45 includes speculation about stress response that, while reasonable, goes beyond what GSEA alone can demonstrate.

results.result: Breast cancer-associated missense mutations in RUNX1 lead to loss-of-function by disrupting DNA binding either directly (affecting DNA contact residues) or indirectly (disrupting RUNT domain fold or CBFβ binding).
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 are based on structural inference from a previous mutagenesis study (Li et al., 2003) rather than direct functional testing in this manuscript. While the inference is reasonable given the structural data cited, the authors did not experimentally validate that these specific mutations cause loss of DNA binding. The conclusion is well-supported by prior work but represents inference rather than new experimental evidence.

results.result: MMTV-Cre;Runx1L/L;R26Y dams exhibited nursing defects with complete failure to wean pups, which died within 24 hours postpartum without milk spots. Histological examination revealed milk stasis and increased cytoplasmic lipid droplets, likely due to disrupted RUNX1 function in myoepithelial cells where Runx1 is exclusively expressed during lactation.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 document a clear phenotype with appropriate controls (C35-C36) and histological validation (C37). The inference that defects are due to myoepithelial dysfunction (C38) is reasonable given Runx1 expression pattern during lactation, though the authors acknowledge additional studies are needed. The phenotype is consistent and reproducible across multiple litters.

results.result: RUNX1 knockdown stable cell lines could only be established in TP53-mutant T47D cells but not in TP53-WT MCF7 cells, suggesting a genetic interaction between RUNX1-loss and TP53-loss operates in human ER+ luminal breast cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 report an observation (C76) and inference (C77). While the inability to generate RUNX1 knockdown in MCF7 cells is noted, the manuscript does not provide details on the number of attempts, methods used, or whether this reflects selection against RUNX1 loss or technical issues. The inference of genetic interaction (C77) is reasonable but speculative without more rigorous experimental validation.

results.result: RUNX1 does not appear to regulate Esr1 transcription directly. While ERα protein was reduced upon RUNX1 knockdown in T47D cells, Esr1 upregulation in vivo appears restricted to ER+ luminal cells and likely reflects hyperproliferation of rescued cells rather than direct transcriptional regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C104 and C131 present a negative result supported by multiple lines of reasoning: lack of consistent Esr1 downregulation in vivo, cell-type-specific upregulation patterns inconsistent with direct repression, and evidence that upregulation correlates with hyperproliferation. The authors appropriately distinguish between in vitro effects (likely indirect through ELF5) and in vivo observations.

results.result: Pathway signatures of RB1, TP53, and RUNX1 mutations are co-associated with human luminal B breast tumors, and >50% of luminal breast cancer cases with RUNX1 mutations are accompanied by mutations or deletions in either TP53 or RB1 genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are based on analysis of published sequencing data (Ellis et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012). While the authors did not generate these data, their analysis of co-occurrence patterns is straightforward and provides important context for the genetic rescue experiments. The >50% co-occurrence is a specific quantitative claim that can be verified from TCGA data.

results.result: RUNX1 is a key regulator of ER+ luminal MECs that controls cell fate by repressing the alveolar program (Elf5) and optimizing the mature luminal program (Foxa1). Loss of RUNX1 impairs ER+ luminal cell fate, but this defect is rescued by Trp53 or Rb1 loss, leading to hyperproliferation that may progress to ER+ luminal breast cancer upon acquisition of additional mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113, C123, C139 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental results. The conclusion that RUNX1 is a key regulator is well-supported by the expression, knockout, and rescue data. The mechanistic model involving Elf5 repression and Foxa1 regulation is supported by ChIP and expression data. The speculation about cancer progression (C112, C139) is appropriately qualified and consistent with human mutation patterns, though it represents a model rather than demonstrated fact.

results.result: RUNX1 and ELF5 function as mutually antagonistic master regulators of ductal versus alveolar cell fates, with RUNX1 repressing ELF5 (this study) and ELF5 reciprocally repressing RUNX1 (prior work), forming a regulatory circuit analogous to the GATA1-PU.1 paradigm in hematopoiesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C81 and C113 integrate current findings with prior work (Kalyuga et al., 2012) to propose a mutual antagonism model. The current study provides strong evidence for RUNX1 repression of ELF5, and the cited work demonstrated the reciprocal relationship. The analogy to GATA1-PU.1 is appropriate given the mutual repression and cell fate determination roles, though the mechanistic details may differ.

results.result: RUNX1 may play an oncogenic role in ER− breast cancers through repression of ELF5 in basal cells, potentially leading to de-repression of SNAI2 (SLUG), which could explain the nursing defect observed in Runx1-null mice similar to Snai2-null mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 present a speculative model connecting RUNX1 expression in ER− breast cancer to potential oncogenic function through the RUNX1→ELF5→SNAI2 axis. While the individual components are supported by citations (C117-C118, C120-C121), the proposed mechanism (C119, C122) is highly speculative and not directly tested. The parallel between Runx1-null and Snai2-null nursing defects is intriguing but circumstantial.

results.result: Loss of Runx1 leads to a crippled ER program through de-repression of Elf5 and insufficient Foxa1 upregulation, causing cellular stress and p53 pathway activation. Loss of Trp53 or Rb1 relieves cell cycle arrest and/or rescues apoptosis, allowing RUNX1-mutant ER+ luminal cells to proliferate and potentially progress to cancer with additional mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C135 present a mechanistic model integrating multiple lines of evidence: GSEA showing p53 pathway enrichment (C45), expression changes in key genes (C48-C49, C91), and genetic rescue data (C70-C72). The model is logical and consistent with the data, though some aspects (particularly the stress response and apoptosis) are inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The speculation about cancer progression (C135) is appropriately qualified.

results.result: RUNX1 was recently identified as a novel mutated gene in human luminal breast cancers through whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing studies, with mutations in CBFB also identified in luminal breast cancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C12-C13, C43 accurately cite recent sequencing studies (Banerji et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Ellis et al., 2012) that identified RUNX1 and CBFB mutations specifically in luminal breast cancers. These are factual statements about prior work that provide important context for the current study.
